evidence.snippet: Late-onset Pompe disease (LOPD) is a rare autosomal recessive glycogen storage disease that results in accumulation of glycogen in muscle cells causing muscular weakness.

nodes.description: Skeletal myofibers in Pompe disease develop large autophagic areas alongside glycogen-filled lysosomes. These areas trap endocytosed recombinant human GAA in a partially processed form so that it never reaches the lysosome, which is a mechanistic explanation for why enzyme replacement therapy is far more effective in cardiac than in skeletal muscle and why it slows rather than arrests the LOPD myopathy. Because LOPD is a decades-long disease treated for decades, this therapeutic ceiling is a defining clinical problem of the late-onset form.

nodes.description: A minority of adults with LOPD develop an arteriopathy whose best-characterized expression is dilatation of the ascending thoracic aorta. It is distinct from the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy of infantile-onset disease - the LOPD myocardium is typically spared - and it is specific enough to LOPD that GeneReviews adds aortic assessment to the annual echocardiogram for this group. Its mechanism is now curated on this entry: it is the aortic expression of the dilative arteriopathy node, downstream of lysosomal glycogen storage in vascular smooth muscle. That causal step is recorded as PROVISIONAL rather than established - see the arteriopathy node and the Gaa-/- mouse link for the evidence that qualifies it.

nodes.description: Progressive dilatation, ectasia and aneurysm formation affecting the ascending thoracic aorta and the intracranial arteries, with the vertebrobasilar system most often involved, together with a small-vessel component that shows up as white matter hyperintensity and cerebellar and brainstem microbleeds. It is the second organ system LOPD damages after muscle, and it is largely uncoupled from myopathy severity: patients are identified on surveillance imaging rather than by limb weakness, and enzyme replacement therapy did not change vessel calibre over a year of follow-up in the one series that looked. The node is recorded as PROVISIONAL rather than ESTABLISHED because the causal step from smooth-muscle glycogen to wall weakness is inferred rather than demonstrated - one aortic specimen showed connective-tissue changes resembling a fibrillinopathy rather than a storage lesion, and the Gaa-/- mouse accumulates little aortic glycogen, which led that study's authors to decline to attribute aortic wall weakness to glycogen accumulation (see animal_models).

nodes.description: Intravenous recombinant human GAA is the standard disease-modifying treatment. nodes.description: The most widely used Pompe mouse, a global Gaa knockout that survives into adulthood without treatment. This entry curates the study that characterized its smooth muscle rather than its skeletal muscle, because that is what bears on the extra-muscular arms of LOPD. Glycogen, lysosomes and autophagosomes accumulate across aortic, tracheal, esophageal, gastric and bladder smooth muscle, with the gastrointestinal and genitourinary tissues most affected. The model's central limitation for late-onset disease is genetic: a global null has essentially no residual enzyme, whereas LOPD is defined by partial activity from a leaky splice allele, so the mouse is genotypically closer to infantile-onset disease and its tempo cannot be read across.

nodes.description: Enzyme replacement therapy changes the trajectory of LOPD but does not normalize it. Walking distance and forced vital capacity improve modestly relative to placebo in the short term, yet muscle fat fraction continues to increase, some patients still progress to ventilatory support, and the effect on sleep-disordered breathing is undocumented. This residual disease burden is a mechanistic consequence of the autophagic mistargeting node and, possibly, of the motor neuron arm of diaphragm weakness, which intravenous enzyme cannot reach.

nodes.description: The LOPD-defining lesion is partial rather than complete loss of acid alpha-glucosidase. The commonest LOPD allele, c.-32-13T>G (IVS1), sits in intron 1 and weakens the splice acceptor of GAA exon 2. Most transcripts from that allele are aberrantly spliced (partial or complete exon 2 skipping), but a low level of correctly spliced, fully functional transcript escapes. That residual activity - conventionally quoted as roughly 1-30% of normal, though see the caveat in the biochemical section and in notes - is what shifts the phenotype from infantile to late onset. In the great majority of LOPD patients the leaky allele is carried in trans with a second, more deleterious pathogenic variant, so the leaky allele is the one setting how much enzyme the patient makes.

nodes.description: Residual GAA activity is exhausted in smooth muscle as well as in skeletal muscle. Autopsy of a woman with LOPD demonstrated lysosomal glycogen inside vascular smooth muscle cells by transmission electron microscopy, alongside involvement of the bladder, intestine, and esophagus. This is a distinct cellular compartment from the skeletal and respiratory myofiber storage that dominates the LOPD clinical picture, and it is the substrate for the disease's two extra-muscular arms: the dilative arteriopathy of large arteries, and the gastrointestinal and genitourinary symptoms that patients report independently of limb weakness. Smooth-muscle storage is the reason LOPD is a systemic lysosomal disease rather than a pure myopathy.

nodes.description: Non-invasive ventilation is the mainstay of treatment for sleep-disordered breathing and ventilatory failure in LOPD, targeting adequate ventilation during sleep and prevention of acute hypercapnic decompensation. evidence.snippet: The mainstay of treatment for SDB and respiratory failure in LOPD is non-invasive ventilation (NIV), which aims to ensure adequate ventilation, particularly during sleep, and prevent acute hypercapnic failure.

nodes.description: Diaphragm weakness in LOPD is disproportionate to limb weakness and is the proximate cause of nocturnal hypoventilation and ultimately of ventilatory failure. Neurophysiological study of treated LOPD patients found that those with respiratory failure had absent or severely reduced phrenic nerve compound muscle action potentials and diaphragm EMG showing neurogenic as well as myopathic changes, implicating spinal phrenic motor neuron dysfunction alongside myofiber disease. Because intravenous recombinant enzyme does not cross the blood-brain barrier, a motor neuron contribution would explain residual respiratory decline on enzyme replacement therapy. The motor neuron arm is curated as PROVISIONAL: the supporting series is small (eight patients) and calls for confirmation.

nodes.description: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing combined with spatial transcriptomics of LOPD muscle biopsies shows that myofibers are transcriptionally abnormal before they are histologically abnormal. Fibers that are not yet vacuolated already show reduced glycolytic gene expression with increased lipid and amino-acid metabolism, upregulated autophagy genes, and downregulated ribosomal and mitochondrial programmes producing defective oxidative phosphorylation. Inflammation, apoptosis, and regeneration signatures appear only once vacuolation is established. This staging matters for LOPD specifically, because it identifies an early, possibly still-tractable metabolic derangement that precedes the structural damage enzyme replacement therapy cannot undo. The study reports only a "tendency" for therapy to restore the dysregulated metabolism, so reversibility is a hypothesis this node raises rather than a result it records.

evidence.snippet: The expression of the genes involved in glycolysis was reduced, whereas the expression of the genes involved in the metabolism of lipids and amino acids was increased in non-vacuolated fibres, indicating early metabolic abnormalities.

nodes.description: Chronic storage and autophagic injury destroy myofibers, which are replaced by fat. The distribution is characteristically limb-girdle and axial, with early involvement of the psoas and paraspinal muscles; quantitative fat fraction on lumbar MRI correlates with strength, walking distance, stair climbing and supine spirometry, and continues to rise during enzyme replacement therapy.

nodes.description: Absence of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a defining feature of LOPD and part of its formal case definition, not merely a statistical tendency. Residual GAA activity is sufficient to keep cardiomyocyte glycogen storage subclinical, so the cardiorespiratory collapse that kills untreated infants does not occur; the respiratory system, not the heart, becomes the life-limiting organ. This node is curated as a mechanistic contrast rather than as a claim that the myocardium is entirely normal - adult arteriopathy and rare conduction findings are described in the umbrella Pompe disease entry.

nodes.description: Respiratory muscle weakness, principally of the diaphragm, progresses to ventilatory failure and is the leading cause of death in untreated LOPD. In roughly a third of patients respiratory symptoms are the presenting complaint, ahead of limb weakness.
nodes.id: Respiratory insufficiency due to muscle weakness

evidence.reference_title: Respiratory failure and sleep-disordered breathing in late-onset Pompe disease: a narrative review.
evidence.snippet: It causes a progressive proximal myopathy, accompanied by respiratory muscle weakness, which can lead to ventilatory failure. In untreated LOPD, the most common cause of death is respiratory failure.

evidence.reference_title: Pompe Disease.
evidence.snippet: Respiratory insufficiency progressing to respiratory failure is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality.

evidence.reference_title: Respiratory failure and sleep-disordered breathing in late-onset Pompe disease: a narrative review.
evidence.snippet: Approximately half will suffer respiratory involvement during the course of their illness

evidence.reference_title: Respiratory failure and sleep-disordered breathing in late-onset Pompe disease: a narrative review.
evidence.snippet: One-third of patients present with respiratory symptoms as their first manifestation of the illness

nodes.description: Acute cerebral infarction or intracranial hemorrhage occurs in a minority of LOPD adults and may be the presenting event. It is the clinically consequential endpoint of the intracranial arteriopathy and the reason vascular imaging is proposed as routine workup in this group.

evidence.reference_title: Intracranial vasculopathy: an important organ damage in young adult patients with late-onset Pompe disease.
evidence.snippet: Seven patients (7/30) had acute cerebral infarction or hemorrhage.

evidence.reference_title: Abnormalities of cerebral arteries are frequent in patients with late-onset Pompe disease.
evidence.snippet: Two patients had clinical signs related to the arteriopathy, including partial paralysis of the third cranial nerve and transient ischemic attacks.

nodes.description: Urinary incontinence in LOPD is attributed to lysosomal glycogen storage in bladder smooth muscle demonstrated at autopsy, rather than to pelvic floor weakness secondary to the limb-girdle myopathy.

evidence.reference_title: Autopsy findings in late-onset Pompe disease: a case report and systematic review of the literature.
evidence.snippet: explaining reports of symptoms such as urinary incontinence and dysphagia

nodes.description: Elongation and dilatation of the vertebrobasilar arteries is the single most common vascular abnormality in LOPD and is usually asymptomatic until it is looked for. Basilar artery diameter correlates with disease duration, so it behaves as a progressive manifestation rather than a static malformation.

evidence.reference_title: Intracranial vasculopathy: an important organ damage in young adult patients with late-onset Pompe disease.
evidence.snippet: Dilative arteriopathy was found in 19 patients (19/30), with vertebrobasilar dolichoectasia found in 17 patients and dilatation of the anterior circulation arteries found in 8 patients.

evidence.reference_title: Intracranial vasculopathy: an important organ damage in young adult patients with late-onset Pompe disease.
evidence.snippet: The maximum diameter of the basilar artery was correlated with disease duration

evidence.reference_title: Abnormalities of cerebral arteries are frequent in patients with late-onset Pompe disease.
evidence.snippet: Four out of six patients had brain vascular anomalies including dolichoectasia of the basilar artery and ectasia of internal carotids.

nodes.description: Intron-1 variant 13 nucleotides upstream of GAA exon 2. It weakens the exon 2 splice acceptor, causing partial and complete exon 2 skipping, while permitting a low level of correctly spliced wild-type transcript - the "leaky" behaviour that yields residual enzyme and late-onset disease.

evidence.reference_title: Antisense Oligonucleotides Promote Exon Inclusion and Correct the Common c.-32-13T>G GAA Splicing Variant in Pompe Disease.
evidence.snippet: which weakens the splice acceptor of GAA exon 2 and induces partial and complete exon 2 skipping. It also allows a low level of leaky wild-type splicing, leading to a childhood/adult phenotype.
